newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo dizzies Argentina with corruption charges.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo dizzies Argentina with corruption charges.

text.p: Argentina's once all powerful Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo has launched a one-man assault on official corruption and no one knows where it will all lead.

Cavallo was fired by President Carlos Menem in July. But he has since probably received as many newspaper column inches as when he held power, with a stream of headline-grabbing accusations against cabinet ministers, deputies and judges.

With some rare exceptions, usually politicians, Argentines mainly assume a good proportion of their leaders and judges are corrupt and dishonest. But the torrent of charges pouring from Cavallo has dizzied even the most cynical.
He has accused Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan of manipulating judges and blocking investigations into graft.

He said Menem's chief of staff Alberto Kohan knew about bribes to win a $250 million state contract but failed to act, and he has raised doubts about the wealth of the leader of the lower house of Congress, Alberto Pierri.
Corach, Jassan and Kohan denied his charges. Corach is suing him, and Pierri has said he will sue.

Launching himself as an alternative political force with an eye to presidential elections in 1999 or 2003, the 50-year old Cavallo has hijacked the mantle of opposition to Menem's Peronist Party from the Radical Party and leftish Frepaso.

The government appears uncertain how to react and generally avoids firing back at his bombshells, apparently hoping the renegade former minister will sink under the weight of the ever greater number of legal proceedings against him.

Cavallo has run up more than 20 libel actions, including one lodged by businessman Alfredo Yabran, whom Cavallo sees as the godfather controlling a network of "mafias" which have infiltrated the state and defend a web of business interests.
So far Cavallo has provided no firm proof for his myriad allegations. Analysts, including some of Cavallo's friends, are unsure if his accusations will have much more effect than landing him in jail.

"Most people think what he says is basically the truth and also seem rather in love with the accusations, but they don't want them taken literally as they are afraid of the implications," said political columnist James Neilson.

"If everything functioned properly all this would inevitably lead to the impeachment of the president and all his ministers," Neilson said, adding, "No one in government, business or the opposition wants this to happen. They want the government to reform but without traumatic upheavals."
The sheer number of charges, and the way the Cavallo has presented them, may also be diminishing their impact.

"What he is doing is demented," said one friend and associate of Cavallo's in private, "It is self-destruction. You can't fight on all fronts at once. You can't fight everyone without their punching back from every side."

Rosendo Fraga, a respected political consultant, recently told his clients he expects Cavallo to be jailed by April. Libel usually means a suspended sentence in Argentina, but piling up several convictions would force him to serve time.
